audits.derivedAnswer: E: 67. The possible areas are 9/5 and 5/3, whose sum is 52/15.
audits.mathematicalReason: Let a and b be the positive horizontal and vertical components of the unit square's upper edge, and let L be the outer square's side. The indicated boundary contacts give a²+b²=1 and L=3a+b=2a+4b. Thus a=3b, b=1/√10, and L=√10. Multiply all lengths by √10 and place the outer square at [0,10]×[0,10]. The unit square's vertex shared with R is W=(4,7), and the upper long edge of the 1-by-3 rectangle has equation x+3y=19. Write R's top and right vertices as P=(p,10) and Q=(10,q). Its fourth vertex is N=W+Q−P=(14−p,q−3). Requiring N to lie on the long edge gives 3q−p=14. Perpendicular adjacent sides give (p−4)(10−p)+3(q−10)=0. Substitution yields (p−7)(p−8)=0. Both roots give vertices within the specified segments. The scaled areas are 18 and 50/3, so the original areas are 9/5 and 5/3. Rectangle properties and rectangle area are appropriate assessed scopes. Coordinate orthogonality and similarity of right projection triangles are alternative valid ways to obtain the same equations.

figureEvidence.fact: The unit square has consecutive vertices on the left boundary, top boundary, in the interior, and at the shared vertex with the 1-by-3 rectangle. The latter rectangle's other vertices lie on the left, bottom, and right boundaries.
R shares the unit square's right-hand interior vertex, has vertices on the outer square's top and right sides, and has its remaining vertex on the upper long edge of the 1-by-3 rectangle.

routes.label: Extend EH and compare triangle areas

audits.mathematicalReason: The four unit-area regions partition the square, so its area is 4 and its side is 2. Set t=AE=AH>0. Triangle AEH has area t²/2=1, giving t=√2. Extend EH to meet the line BC at K below B. Because AEH is right isosceles, BK=BE=2−√2. Triangle KFI is right at I and has a 45° angle at K, so IK=FI and its area is FI²/2. Triangle KBE has area (2−√2)²/2. Their difference is precisely quadrilateral BFIE, whose area is 1. Hence FI²/2−(2−√2)²/2=1, giving FI²=8−4√2. This directly supports the triangle-area and composite-area assessment. The isosceles-triangle route is valid; coordinates, line intersections, shoelace area, and point-to-line distance also provide a valid alternative.

figureEvidence.fact: E, F, G, and H lie on successive sides of ABCD, and EH together with FI and GJ partitions the square into the four named regions.
I lies between E and H, and the right-angle mark at I identifies FI as perpendicular to EH. Extending EH past E meets the extension of BC below B.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let the triangle's altitude be H>5 and its base be B. The squares' upper edges are parallel cross-sections of widths 3 and 2 at heights 3 and 5 above the base. Similar apex triangles therefore give (H−3)/(H−5)=3/2, so H=9. Comparing the full triangle with the triangle above the larger square gives B/3=9/6, hence B=9/2. The area is BH/2=81/4=20¼. Applying corresponding-length ratios in similar triangles and then the triangle-area formula matches the assessed scopes; establishing similarity, segment arithmetic, and solving the linear equation are appropriate support.

figureEvidence.fact: The larger square rests on the triangle's base, with its upper corners on the sloping sides. The smaller square rests on the larger square's upper edge and also has its upper corners on the sloping sides.
The two squares have parallel horizontal upper edges, giving full triangle cross-sections at heights 3 and 3+2=5; no proportions are inferred from the drawing's scale.

audits.derivedAnswer: D: 145/147 of the field is planted.
audits.mathematicalReason: Let s be the unplanted square's side and P its corner opposite the field's right-angle vertex. With the legs on the positive coordinate axes, the hypotenuse is 3x+4y=12. Its distance from points of the square is minimized at P=(s,s), so the given shortest distance is the perpendicular height from P to the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse has length 5. Joining P to the triangle's three vertices partitions the field into triangles of areas 5·2/2, 3s/2, and 4s/2. Thus 6=5+7s/2, giving s=2/7. The planted fraction is (6−s²)/6=1−2/147=145/147. Equivalently, the coordinate distance equation is (12−7s)/5=2. Both routes are valid alternatives, and the assessed distance and composite-area scopes are appropriate.

figureEvidence.fact: S occupies the right-angle corner with two sides along the triangle's legs. The segment labeled 2 joins its opposite corner to the hypotenuse.
The triangle's full legs are labeled 3 and 4. The perpendicular interpretation of the segment of length 2 follows from the stem's shortest-distance condition, not merely its drawn angle.

audits.mathematicalReason: The triangular array has six symmetries: the identity, two nontrivial rotations, and three reflections. There are 6·C(5,2)=60 labeled paintings, choosing the green position and then the two red positions. Neither nontrivial rotation fixes a painting because it has no fixed disk position for the unique green disk. Each reflection fixes two positions and exchanges two pairs. A fixed painting puts green at one fixed position, blue at the other fixed position and at one exchanged pair, and red at the remaining pair. Thus each reflection fixes 2·2=4 paintings. Averaging fixed counts gives (60+3·4)/6=12. This accounts for the smaller orbits of reflection-symmetric paintings and fits the symmetry-counting definition, with combinations as valid support.

figureEvidence.fact: The six congruent disks form an equilateral triangular array with three corner positions and three side-midpoint positions. Its rotations preserve these two position types, and each reflection fixes one position of each type while swapping the other four positions in pairs.

audits.mathematicalReason: Reading the bars for 1 through 7 days gives frequencies 1, 3, 2, 6, 8, 3, and 2. There are 25 students and 1·1+2·3+3·2+4·6+5·8+6·3+7·2=109 total reported exercise-days. The frequency-weighted mean is 109/25=4.36 days, already expressed to the nearest hundredth. Weighted mean is the appropriate assessed procedure, and reading bar heights is appropriate support.

figureEvidence.fact: The horizontal axis gives exercise-day values 1–7, and the corresponding bar heights on the student-count axis are 1, 3, 2, 6, 8, 3, and 2.

audits.mathematicalReason: Model each face as a vertex and each shared edge as adjacency. Each five-face ring forms a cycle. Each upper-ring face has two lower-ring neighbors, in addition to its two same-ring neighbors and the top face. A permitted path chooses its first upper-ring face in 5 ways and must cross to the lower ring exactly once. Starting at a fixed face in a five-cycle, a non-repeating ring path has one possibility using zero edges and two possibilities for each length 1, 2, 3, or 4, totaling 9. There are then 2 choices for the crossing and 9 choices for the lower-ring path before moving to the bottom face. The count is 5·9·2·9=810. Graph modeling and combined addition/multiplication counting match the candidate scopes; no quotient by rotational symmetry is requested.

figureEvidence.fact: The pictured solid has pentagonal faces joined along edges. Moves use shared-edge face adjacency, not contact only at a vertex.

Using the regular dodecahedron specified in the stem, the slanted faces form two five-face cycles. Each slanted face has one horizontal-face neighbor, two same-ring neighbors, and two opposite-ring neighbors; hidden incidences are determined by that specified solid rather than by measuring the perspective drawing.

audits.mathematicalReason: For an n-step staircase, the horizontal runs contain n, n, n−1, …, 1 toothpicks, totaling n+n(n+1)/2=n(n+3)/2. The vertical count is identical, so the total is n(n+3). This gives 18 when n=3, as stated. Setting n(n+3)=180 yields n²+3n−180=(n+15)(n−12)=0. Since the step count is a positive integer, n=12; the negative root is inadmissible. Deriving the expression for the geometric pattern is the assessed procedure. Arithmetic-series summation supports this derivation, and factoring and the quadratic formula are both defensible alternative solution routes.

figureEvidence.fact: The staircase consists of square cells in rows of lengths 3, 2, and 1, with shared cell edges represented by a single toothpick. Its horizontal runs have lengths 3, 3, 2, and 1, and its vertical runs have the same lengths.
